title: How I built a set of free salary calculators with React, Vite and TypeScript
excerpt: I recently built SalaryPayTools, a small site of free US pay calculators. Here is a short write-up of how it is put together and
content:
I recently built SalaryPayTools, a small site of free US pay calculators. Here is a short write-up of how it is put together and what I learned.

What it does

There are 14 calculators: hourly to salary and salary to hourly, annual income, weekly, biweekly and monthly pay, part-time pay, overtime, pay raise, a basic 2026 federal income tax estimate, and 2026 take-home pay for four states (Texas, Arkansas, Illinois and North Carolina). They are free and need no signup.

The stack

React + Vite + TypeScript. Vite keeps the dev loop fast, and TypeScript helps because many pay-calculator bugs are unit mix-ups: hourly vs. annual, weekly vs. biweekly, a percentage stored as 5 instead of 0.05.

Keep the math in plain functions

The calculators are mostly forms on top of small, pure functions. A simplified sketch of the idea (not the site's exact code):

type HourlyInput = {
  rate: number;
  hoursPerWeek: number;
  weeksPerYear: number;
  overtimeHours: number;
  overtimeMultiplier: number; // 1.5 for time-and-a-half
};

export function annualGross(i: HourlyInput): number {
  const weekly =
    i.rate * i.hoursPerWeek +
    i.rate * i.overtimeHours * i.overtimeMultiplier;
  return weekly * i.weeksPerYear;
}

Functions like this are easy to test with known answers before any UI exists. For example, $20 an hour × 40 hours × 52 weeks should always give $41,600.

Show the formula next to the answer

Every result on the site shows how it was calculated, e.g. ($20.00 × 40) × 52 paid weeks. A number you can't check is hard to trust, so the formula is always right there.

One page per calculator

Each calculator has its own URL and its own HTML page with the content already in it, so the page isn't empty before JavaScript loads. That helps both search engines and slow phones.

Be clear about scope

The federal tax tool is a basic estimate, and take-home pay is only for the four states above. I'd rather say that plainly than pretend to cover everything.

If you want to try it or check my math: salarypaytools.com. Feedback is welcome.

title: Investigating a traffic spike with Vercel Analytics and first-party events
excerpt:
A traffic spike on a small website can be surprisingly difficult to explain.

On October 28, my text graphics tool, GummyType, r
content:
A traffic spike on a small website can be surprisingly difficult to explain.

On October 28, my text graphics tool, GummyType, received a sudden increase in visits. I hadn't run a campaign or a batch test.

I used three sources to investigate:

  • Vercel Web Analytics.
  • First-party event records stored in Upstash Redis.
  • Vercel request logs and firewall data.

Each answered a different question.

1. Separate visitors, sessions, events, and requests

A Vercel snapshot showed 111 visitors and 236 page views over the previous 24 hours.

My event logs covered a separate, narrower window: approximately 17:32–17:53, Beijing time.

That window contained:

Metric Count
Session IDs 81
Page-view events 177
Sessions containing only one page-view event 55
Sessions with a completed PNG export 2

These numbers describe different things.

My session ID is stored in sessionStorage and expires after 30 minutes without a recorded event. It isn't a persistent identifier for a person.

Likewise, CDN requests include resources such as images and scripts. Thousands of requests don't mean thousands of visitors.

2. Read “direct” as missing attribution

My source classification includes this check:

if (!referrer) return "direct";

That is the meaning of direct in my implementation: no referring page was available when the session started.

It doesn't identify a channel.

A copied link, an app opening a URL, or automation navigating directly could all produce missing attribution. The label alone cannot distinguish them.

3. Check browser information separately

The strongest additional clue came from Vercel's browser breakdown.

A later snapshot classified 44 visitors, approximately 40%, as using WeChat.

Two sampled homepage requests contained different WeChat versions in their user-agent strings:

MicroMessenger/8.0.62
MicroMessenger/8.0.79

This supported WeChat usage as an explanation for part of the traffic.

It did not reveal the original message, group, or article. User-agent information is also a clue rather than proof of a human visitor.

Browser type and referring source answer different questions. A visit can be classified as WeChat in one report and direct in another without contradiction.

4. Separate suspicious browsing from attack evidence

Some sessions switched pages rapidly. One recorded 17 page views in roughly a minute.

The firewall also showed requests for paths such as:

/.env
/wp-admin/install.php
/phpinfo.php

Those probes were suspicious, but I couldn't establish that they belonged to the same activity as the analytics spike.

At the time I checked server health, Vercel reported 0% function errors and 0% timeouts.

Another distinction matters here: several GET requests close together can include framework prefetching. They don't necessarily represent someone viewing every requested page. Client-side page-view events provide different evidence.

5. Identify what the instrumentation cannot answer

My export flow records an attempt ID across stages such as:

png_export_started
png_generated
png_export_completed

That helps distinguish an export attempt from a page visit.

However, ordinary text edits and style changes weren't fully tracked. A session with one page-view event could still have spent time experimenting without exporting.

Also, a completed export event reports the browser delivery outcome. It doesn't independently verify that a file was saved to disk.

The conclusion remains incomplete

I found evidence of WeChat visits, rapid browsing, and unrelated-looking vulnerability probes.

I did not find enough evidence to label the entire spike as organic growth or an attack.

The next useful instrumentation step is a once-per-session interaction event for the first text or style edit, without collecting the user's text.

That would make the funnel clearer:

Page opened → Tool edited → Export completed

The investigation helped me narrow the possibilities. It also exposed where my data stops being able to answer the question.

Disclosure: I used AI assistance to analyze the data and draft this article. The figures describe snapshots collected on October 28, 2026.

title: I got tired of Postman using 1GB RAM, so I built Ghostman (TUI API Client)
excerpt:
Hi everyone,

Like many developers, I got frustrated with what happened to Postman: it turned from a simple dev tool into a 1GB+ Electron app that forces cloud accounts, team workspaces, and
content:
Hi everyone,

Like many developers, I got frustrated with what happened to Postman: it turned from a simple dev tool into a 1GB+ Electron app that forces cloud accounts, team workspaces, and telemetry just to test an endpoint.

So I built Ghostman — a lightweight, keyboard-first terminal API studio that respects your system and privacy.

Why use Ghostman over Postman?

  1. RAM & Startup:
  2. Postman: Uses 800MB - 1.5GB RAM, slow to start.

  3. Ghostman: Takes ~40MB, starts in under 200ms right in your terminal.

  4. Cloud & Privacy:

  5. Postman: Pushes your collections to the cloud, requires login.

  6. Ghostman: 100% Local-First. Collections live in plain YAML (.ghostman/collections.yaml) inside your repo. Commit it to Git with your team. Zero accounts, zero tracking.

  7. Built-in Webhook Receiver (The Killer Feature):

  8. Postman: Testing incoming webhooks (Stripe, GitHub, Discord) requires setting up external tunnels (ngrok) or web mock tools.

  9. Ghostman: Hit Ctrl+W and it instantly spins up a local receiver on port 9090. Incoming HTTP callbacks show up live on your screen.

  10. Keyboard-Driven Workflow:

  11. Complete requests, inspect formatted JSON responses, and view latency telemetry (ms) without taking your hands off the keyboard.

It is 100% open source under the MIT License (screenshots in the repo):
https://github.com/4yk5/Ghostman

If you find it useful, feel free to give it a star or share your feedback!

title: I asked eight models which clubs footballers played for
excerpt: ExtraTime, my football quiz site, has a database of footballers and every club they played for, checked by hand, because the games depend on it. Career Path shows you a player's clubs and you guess
content:
ExtraTime, my football quiz site, has a database of footballers and every club they played for, checked by hand, because the games depend on it. Career Path shows you a player's clubs and you guess who he is. Five Clubs does the reverse. A wrong club in that data is a wrong answer for whoever's playing.

So when people ask why I don't just have a model generate the questions, I'd like to answer with a number. I picked 200 players from the database, asked eight models which clubs each one played for, and scored every answer against the real list.

The setup

The 200 players are 50 from each of ExtraTime's four Career Path difficulty tiers: EASY, NORMAL, HARD and EXTREME. The tiers are about how well-known a player's career is, so EASY is Fabio Grosso and Teddy Sheringham, and EXTREME is players most fans won't have heard of. Between them the 200 played for 1,292 clubs.

Every model got the same prompt, once per player:

Footballer: Fabio Grosso, born 1977-11-28.

Answer from memory, as JSON only, no other text:
{"known": true or false, "nationality": "the country he represents or is a citizen of", "clubs": ["every senior club he has played for, including loans, in order"]}

If you don't know this player, answer {"known": false} and nothing else. Don't guess clubs you aren't sure of.

The date of birth is there so the model knows which Ronaldo I mean. The last line gives every model a way out, so a model that guesses has chosen to.

All eight ran through DigitalOcean's serverless inference, one endpoint and one API key for models from OpenAI, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral, Google and Anthropic. That made switching models a change to one string, and all 1,600 questions together cost $1.08.

Scoring each club means matching a name like "Internazionale" to ExtraTime's "Inter". I matched against all 5,451 clubs in the database and their 2,337 alternative names, then went through about 150 near-misses by hand and changed 43 of the decisions. "Dinamo Bucharest", "Cologne" and "Chealsea" count as right. "Lazio Roma" for a Roma player doesn't.

Results

Precision is the share of the clubs a model named that were really the player's. Recall is the share of the player's 1,292 real clubs that the model named. A player it declined to answer counts as zero recall. "All right" means every club listed, and nothing wrong added.

Model Precision Recall All right Said "don't know" Nationality Cost, 200 players Median time
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 76% 69% 50 6 186/194 $0.526 20.3 s
Llama 4 Maverick 75% 50% 18 13 172/185 $0.012 1.9 s
gpt-oss-120b 63% 32% 13 45 145/155 $0.090 9.9 s
GPT-5.4 mini 62% 58% 22 9 188/191 $0.060 1.3 s
Gemma 4 31B 49% 23% 4 48 133/149 $0.009 2.5 s
Claude Haiku 4.5 44% 30% 4 57 136/143 $0.081 1.4 s
gpt-oss-20b 33% 6% 1 129 67/71 $0.079 7.7 s
Ministral 3 14B 14% 9% 1 23 119/152 $0.007 1.0 s

No model is good enough to write quiz answers on its own. The best one got a quarter of its clubs wrong, and it got every club right for only 50 of the 200 players.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash was the most accurate and the slowest by far. It's a reasoning model, and it spent a median of about 1,600 tokens thinking per answer, so the median answer took 20 seconds and one in ten took more than 66. GPT-5.4 mini named the most clubs, 1,216, and answered in 1.3 seconds. Llama 4 Maverick was as precise as DeepSeek, half as complete, and cost $0.012 for all 200 players. That's about two cents per thousand correct clubs, against 59 cents for DeepSeek.

Ministral 3 14B was wrong six times out of seven. For Grosso, it listed seven clubs, and he played for one of them. For Christian Panucci it invented "Byte CapSelect Roma". And 25 of its answers weren't valid JSON, because it wrote notes inside the array, like "Real Madrid" (loand to "PSV Eindhoven").

Fame is most of it

Precision by tier:

Model EASY NORMAL HARD EXTREME
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 96% 91% 79% 43%
Llama 4 Maverick 92% 79% 73% 53%
GPT-5.4 mini 91% 76% 59% 28%
gpt-oss-120b 81% 58% 59% 33%
Gemma 4 31B 76% 51% 28% 16%
Claude Haiku 4.5 64% 39% 31% 35%
gpt-oss-20b 41% 33% 8% 0%
Ministral 3 14B 30% 10% 7% 7%

On the 50 best-known players, the top three were above 90%. On the 50 least known, the best was 53%. That's exactly the wrong way round for a quiz site. Famous careers are the ones I need help with least.

"Don't guess" didn't stop the guessing

Every model was told to skip players it didn't know. They mostly answered anyway, and the answers on the players they barely knew were where the wrong clubs piled up.

Claude Haiku 4.5 declined 57 players, more than most, and still named 488 clubs that weren't the player's, against 389 that were. gpt-oss-20b was the most cautious. It declined 129 of the 200, including 12 of the 50 easiest. When it did answer, two clubs in three were wrong. Declining more didn't make the answers that were left any better.

The wrong clubs are usually real clubs, which makes them harder to catch. Of the 2,820 clubs the models named that weren't the player's, 2,459 were other clubs in my database, and only 355 didn't match any club at all. A made-up name is easy to spot. Palermo on the wrong player isn't.

When the models agreed and the database didn't

If several models independently name the same club and my database doesn't have it, maybe the database is wrong. Only three player-club pairs were named by four or more of the eight models and missing from the database:

  • Teddy Sheringham at Stevenage, from five models. He never played for them. He managed them in 2015–16, and according to his Wikipedia page he even registered himself as a player, at 49, without making an appearance. The models were remembering the right man at the right club in the wrong role.
  • Loïc Rémy at Rennes, from four. He never played there. Four models were wrong in the same way.
  • Grenddy Perozo at Deportivo Anzoátegui, from four. Here the models were right and my data was wrong: ExtraTime has the club twice, as "Anzoategui" and "Deportivo Anzoategui". His career points at one of them, and the models named the other.

So the database held up, and the test found one real bug in it.

What I got wrong

My first run gave every model 3,000 output tokens. DeepSeek ran out of tokens on 56 of the 200 players while still reasoning, and returned nothing. Those turned out to be mostly the hard players. With them missing, DeepSeek looked 88% precise. I reran the 64 truncated answers (58 DeepSeek, 6 gpt-oss-20b) with 16,000 tokens. Some needed more than 10,000, and DeepSeek's precision fell to 76%. The first attempts cost $0.22 and produced nothing.

My first club matcher counted a club as right if every word of the claim appeared in one of the player's club names. So "AC Milan" matched "Inter Milan", and Grosso picked up a club he never played for. Now an exact match with another real club wins first.

The nationality check was looser than I wanted. A model saying "Spain" for Omar Mascarell, who was born in Spain and plays for Equatorial Guinea, is marked wrong against ExtraTime's data, though it isn't really wrong. I'd treat the nationality column as rough.

Caveats

200 players and one prompt per player, at default temperature. A second run would move individual numbers by a few points. ExtraTime's data is the answer key, so where it has a gap, a correct model answer counts as wrong. The disagreement check above suggests that's rare, but it isn't zero. The tiers measure how well-known a career is for ExtraTime's players, not some general measure of fame. And this tests memory on purpose. With a search tool or the database in the prompt, every model here would do much better.

What I'd take from it

  • Don't let a model write facts into a quiz unchecked. Even the best one here got a quarter of its clubs wrong.
  • Use a model to draft, and check against your own data. Llama 4 Maverick at two cents per thousand correct clubs is cheap enough to draft everything and throw away what doesn't check out.
  • Expect it to be worst exactly where you need help: the obscure players.
  • Telling a model not to guess isn't a control. Measure what it does with the instruction.
  • Give reasoning models enough output tokens, and count the ones that ran out, or your numbers will flatter them.

content:
The Societal Roots of Schadenfreude in Software Engineers' Job Losses: An Analytical Perspective

Impact Chains: Tracing the Pathways of Schadenfreude

The phenomenon of schadenfreude—deriving pleasure from others' misfortunes—manifests in complex ways when applied to job losses in high-paying industries like software engineering. Three distinct impact chains illuminate its psychological and socioeconomic underpinnings:

  • Economic Insecurity -> Triggers zero-sum thinking -> Perception of job loss as personal gain for others

Analysis: Economic instability fosters a zero-sum mindset, where one group's loss is perceived as another's gain. This cognitive framework distorts empathy, positioning software engineers' layoffs as beneficial to other professions, thereby justifying schadenfreude.

  • Media Framing -> Amplifies negative stereotypes -> Public adoption of schadenfreude as a justified response

Analysis: Media narratives often sensationalize layoffs, framing them as consequences of greed or overcompensation. This framing reinforces stereotypes, normalizing schadenfreude as a socially acceptable reaction to perceived injustice.

  • Professional Envy -> Activates social comparison processes -> Expression of schadenfreude toward high-paying professions

Analysis: Social comparison mechanisms drive envy toward high-earning professions. When software engineers face layoffs, this envy transforms into schadenfreude, reflecting a distorted sense of fairness and personal validation.

System Instabilities: The Structural Foundations of Schadenfreude

Underlying these impact chains are systemic instabilities that perpetuate schadenfreude:

  • Misapplication of Meritocracy: Societal norms around fairness are distorted, leading to unjustified attribution of job loss to personal failings.

Analysis: The meritocracy myth, when misapplied, blames individuals for systemic failures. This narrative shifts responsibility onto software engineers, framing their layoffs as deserved outcomes rather than broader economic consequences.

  • Empathy Erosion: Limited personal connection and high-stakes environments reduce empathetic responses, exacerbating schadenfreude.

Analysis: In competitive professional environments, empathy diminishes as self-interest takes precedence. This erosion amplifies schadenfreude, as individuals prioritize personal security over collective solidarity.

  • Media Feedback Loop: Sensationalized narratives reinforce negative attitudes, creating a self-sustaining cycle of public schadenfreude.

Analysis: Media amplification of negative narratives perpetuates schadenfreude by validating and spreading hostile attitudes, further entrenching societal divisions.

Mechanisms and Logic: The Psychological and Socioeconomic Drivers

Four key mechanisms underpin the expression of schadenfreude in this context:

  1. Social Comparison Processes: Individuals evaluate their success relative to software engineers, triggering envy or schadenfreude based on perceived inequality.

Analysis: Social comparison fuels schadenfreude by positioning others' misfortunes as a benchmark for personal success, particularly in professions perceived as privileged.

  1. Cognitive Biases: The just-world hypothesis leads to the belief that job loss is deserved, aligning with societal narratives of meritocracy.

Analysis: This bias reinforces schadenfreude by rationalizing layoffs as just outcomes, ignoring systemic factors and perpetuating individual blame.

  1. Emotional Contagion: Attitudes expressed within social circles are mirrored, spreading schadenfreude through emotional adoption.

Analysis: Emotional contagion amplifies schadenfreude by normalizing it within social networks, creating a culture of hostility toward displaced workers.

  1. Economic Competition: Resource scarcity fosters zero-sum thinking, where software engineers' losses are perceived as gains for other professions.

Analysis: Economic competition exacerbates schadenfreude by framing professional crises as opportunities for personal advancement, undermining collective empathy.

Observable Effects: The Societal Consequences of Schadenfreude

The pervasive attitude of schadenfreude manifests in tangible ways, with significant implications for societal cohesion:

  • Public Statements: Comments like "couldn't have happened to more deserving guys" reflect internalized schadenfreude.

Analysis: Such statements reveal the normalization of schadenfreude, indicating a broader cultural acceptance of hostility toward displaced workers.

  • Media Amplification: Negative framing of layoffs as consequences of greed fuels public schadenfreude.

Analysis: Media narratives shape public perception, reinforcing schadenfreude and hindering empathetic responses to professional crises.

  • Erosion of Solidarity: Economic anxiety and zero-sum thinking reduce collective support for displaced workers.

Analysis: The erosion of solidarity undermines societal resilience, creating a more hostile and less supportive environment during economic challenges.

Intermediate Conclusions and Societal Stakes

The prevalence of schadenfreude toward software engineers' job losses is not merely a psychological quirk but a symptom of deeper societal issues. It reflects systemic envy, economic insecurity, and a distorted understanding of fairness. If unaddressed, this attitude risks:

  • Eroding trust in professional communities
  • Fostering division and hostility in the workplace
  • Undermining collective resilience during economic crises

Reevaluating our perceptions and fostering empathy are not just moral imperatives but essential steps toward building a more cohesive and supportive society. The stakes are clear: without intervention, schadenfreude will continue to corrode the foundations of professional and societal solidarity.

The Psychology and Socioeconomics of Schadenfreude in Software Engineers' Job Losses

Impact Chains: Deconstructing the Phenomenon

The pervasive attitude of schadenfreude in response to software engineers' job losses can be systematically deconstructed into three primary impact chains, each revealing distinct psychological and socioeconomic mechanisms. These chains not only explain the emergence of schadenfreude but also highlight its deeper societal implications.

  • Economic Insecurity → Zero-Sum Thinking → Perceived Personal Gain

Economic instability acts as a catalyst for zero-sum thinking, a cognitive framework where individuals perceive others' losses as opportunities for personal advancement. This process is driven by resource scarcity and economic competition, leading to the observable effect of public expressions of satisfaction with others' misfortune. Such reactions underscore a broader societal anxiety about professional stability, where empathy is often overshadowed by self-preservation.

  • Media Framing → Negative Stereotypes → Justified Schadenfreude

Sensationalized media narratives play a pivotal role in amplifying negative stereotypes about software engineers, often portraying layoffs as consequences of greed or overcompensation. This framing activates cognitive biases, such as the just-world hypothesis, which rationalizes schadenfreude by attributing job losses to perceived moral failings. The result is a normalized hostility toward displaced workers, reflecting a societal tendency to blame individuals rather than systemic issues.

  • Professional Envy → Social Comparison → Expression of Schadenfreude

In highly competitive fields, professional envy triggers social comparison processes, where individuals measure their success against others. This dynamic fosters emotional contagion, leading to the observable effect of schadenfreude expressed within social circles. Such behavior reveals the corrosive impact of envy on professional relationships and the erosion of solidarity in the face of collective challenges.

System Instabilities: Root Causes of Schadenfreude

The persistence of schadenfreude in this context is underpinned by systemic instabilities that exacerbate negative attitudes and behaviors. These instabilities are both a cause and consequence of the impact chains described above, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of hostility and division.

  • Misapplication of Meritocracy

The misapplication of meritocracy leads to the attribution of job losses to individual failings rather than systemic factors. This instability is driven by societal norms and cognitive biases, resulting in unjustified schadenfreude. By ignoring structural issues, society perpetuates a narrative that undermines collective empathy and support for displaced workers.

  • Empathy Erosion

Competitive environments erode empathy, prioritizing self-interest over solidarity. This erosion is exacerbated by economic anxiety and media narratives, leading to reduced collective support for those in crisis. The consequences extend beyond individual attitudes, threatening the fabric of professional communities and societal cohesion.

  • Media Feedback Loop

Sensationalized media narratives create a feedback loop that perpetuates and amplifies schadenfreude. Driven by emotional contagion and social influence, this loop normalizes negative attitudes, making them more acceptable and widespread. The media's role in shaping public perception thus becomes a critical factor in either mitigating or exacerbating schadenfreude.

Mechanisms and Constraints: The Structural Framework

The following table outlines the key mechanisms driving schadenfreude, their constraints, and the observable effects. This framework highlights the interplay between psychological processes, socioeconomic factors, and societal norms, providing a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon.
Mechanism Constraint Observable Effect
Social comparison processes Limited empathy in professional environments Expression of schadenfreude in social circles
Cognitive biases (just-world hypothesis) Misalignment between perceived merit and actual circumstances Public statements justifying layoffs as deserved
Emotional contagion and mirroring Media narratives prioritizing sensationalism Amplification of negative attitudes through social networks
Media framing and narrative construction Lack of systemic support for displaced workers Normalization of hostility toward displaced workers
Economic competition and resource scarcity Societal norms around fairness and meritocracy Zero-sum thinking and perceived personal gain

Physics and Logic of Processes: The Operational Dynamics

The system of schadenfreude operates through distinct processes that transform inputs into outputs, sustained by feedback loops and threshold effects. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for addressing the root causes of schadenfreude and its societal implications.

  1. Input → Processing → Output

Economic insecurity and media narratives serve as inputs, triggering zero-sum thinking and cognitive biases. These processes result in the output of schadenfreude, expressed through public statements and social interactions. This chain reveals how external factors are internalized and manifest as harmful attitudes.

  1. Feedback Loops

Media framing and emotional contagion create feedback loops that amplify negative attitudes and normalize schadenfreude. Sustained by social influence and economic anxiety, these loops perpetuate a cycle of hostility and division, undermining societal resilience.

  1. Threshold Effects

The system exhibits threshold effects, where small changes in economic conditions or media narratives can lead to disproportionate increases in schadenfreude. This nonlinear relationship between resource scarcity and zero-sum thinking highlights the fragility of societal attitudes and the need for proactive intervention.

Intermediate Conclusions and Analytical Pressure

The analysis of schadenfreude in the context of software engineers' job losses reveals a complex interplay of psychological, socioeconomic, and systemic factors. This phenomenon is not merely a reflection of individual attitudes but a symptom of deeper societal issues, including envy, misunderstanding, and economic insecurity. If left unaddressed, schadenfreude risks eroding trust, fostering division, and undermining collective resilience in the face of economic challenges.

The stakes are high: a professional environment characterized by hostility and lack of support will hinder innovation, collaboration, and individual well-being. Addressing schadenfreude requires a reevaluation of how we perceive and support one another during times of crisis, emphasizing empathy, systemic understanding, and responsible media narratives. By doing so, we can foster a more cohesive and resilient society capable of navigating the complexities of the modern economy.

Mechanisms of Schadenfreude in Software Engineers' Job Losses: A Societal Mirror

The phenomenon of schadenfreude—taking pleasure in others' misfortunes—has become disturbingly prevalent in response to job losses among software engineers. This article dissects the psychological and socioeconomic roots of this attitude, revealing it as a symptom of deeper societal issues. By deconstructing the mechanisms at play, we uncover how envy, misunderstanding, and economic insecurity converge to erode empathy and threaten societal cohesion.

Impact Chains: Tracing the Path to Schadenfreude

Schadenfreude in this context is not a spontaneous emotion but the culmination of interconnected processes:

  • Economic Insecurity → Zero-Sum Thinking → Perceived Personal Gain

Economic instability fosters a zero-sum mindset, where individuals view others' job losses as opportunities for personal advancement. This dynamic, driven by resource scarcity and competitive environments, highlights the fragility of economic security and its role in shaping perceptions of fairness.

  • Media Framing → Negative Stereotypes → Justified Schadenfreude

Sensationalized media narratives amplify stereotypes about software engineers, often portraying them as overcompensated or insulated from economic hardship. These narratives activate cognitive biases like the just-world hypothesis, normalizing schadenfreude as a justified response to perceived inequities.

  • Professional Envy → Social Comparison → Expression of Schadenfreude

Competitive professional environments encourage social comparison, particularly in high-paying fields like software engineering. This triggers envy, which manifests as schadenfreude when high-status professions face setbacks, revealing the corrosive effects of unchecked competition on empathy.

System Instabilities: The Foundations of Eroding Empathy

The persistence of schadenfreude is underpinned by systemic instabilities that distort perceptions and erode solidarity:

  • Misapplication of Meritocracy

The belief that job losses reflect personal failings rather than systemic factors perpetuates unjustified schadenfreude. This misalignment between perceived merit and reality underscores the limitations of meritocratic narratives in explaining complex economic outcomes.

  • Empathy Erosion

High-stakes, competitive environments prioritize self-interest over collective well-being, reducing empathy. Exacerbated by economic anxiety, this erosion transforms schadenfreude into a coping mechanism, further fragmenting professional communities.

  • Media Feedback Loop

Sensationalized media narratives create a feedback loop, amplifying negative attitudes through emotional contagion and social influence. This loop sustains schadenfreude, normalizing hostility toward displaced workers and undermining public empathy.

Key Mechanisms and Constraints: The Psychology of Division

Schadenfreude is driven by psychological mechanisms constrained by societal and professional environments:

  • Social Comparison Processes

Individuals evaluate their success relative to others, leading to envy or schadenfreude. This mechanism is constrained by limited empathy in competitive fields, highlighting the tension between individual ambition and collective solidarity.

  • Cognitive Biases

The just-world hypothesis and other biases rationalize layoffs as just outcomes, ignoring systemic factors. This misalignment between perception and reality fuels public justification of schadenfreude, revealing the power of cognitive distortions in shaping attitudes.

  • Economic Competition

Resource scarcity and economic competition drive zero-sum thinking, where one’s loss is perceived as another’s gain. Amplified by societal norms around fairness and meritocracy, this constraint underscores the role of economic systems in fostering division.

Observable Effects: The Societal Cost of Schadenfreude

The consequences of schadenfreude extend beyond individual emotions, manifesting in observable societal effects:

  • Public Statements

Normalized hostility toward displaced workers is reflected in public discourse, as seen in expressions of satisfaction with software engineers' job losses. These statements reveal the depth of societal fragmentation and the erosion of empathy.

  • Media Amplification

Sensationalized narratives shape public perception, hindering empathy and perpetuating schadenfreude through emotional contagion. Media's role in amplifying negative attitudes highlights its influence on societal norms and values.

  • Erosion of Solidarity

Reduced collective support during economic challenges undermines professional communities, fostering division and hostility. This erosion of solidarity threatens the resilience of societies in the face of shared crises.

System Instability Analysis: A Fragile Societal Equilibrium

The prevalence of schadenfreude signals systemic instability, driven by:

  • Feedback Loops

Media framing and emotional contagion create feedback loops that sustain and amplify negative attitudes, perpetuating schadenfreude. These loops highlight the self-reinforcing nature of societal divisions.

  • Threshold Effects

Small changes in economic conditions or media narratives can disproportionately increase schadenfreude, revealing societal fragility. This sensitivity underscores the ease with which negative attitudes can spread and intensify.

  • Empathy Erosion

Competitive environments and economic anxiety reduce empathy, prioritizing self-interest over solidarity. This erosion is a critical instability, as it undermines the collective support systems necessary for societal resilience.

Intermediate Conclusions: Why This Matters

The pervasive attitude of schadenfreude toward software engineers' job losses is not merely a reflection of individual malice but a symptom of broader societal issues. It reveals the corrosive effects of economic insecurity, media influence, and competitive professional environments on empathy and solidarity. If unaddressed, this attitude risks eroding trust, fostering division, and undermining collective resilience, ultimately leading to a more hostile and less supportive professional environment.

Final Analysis: A Call for Reevaluation

Schadenfreude in the context of software engineers' job losses serves as a societal mirror, reflecting deeper issues of envy, misunderstanding, and economic insecurity. Addressing this phenomenon requires a reevaluation of how we perceive and support one another in times of professional crisis. By fostering empathy, challenging cognitive biases, and promoting systemic fairness, we can rebuild the solidarity necessary to navigate economic challenges collectively. The stakes are high: the future of workplace cohesion and societal resilience depends on our ability to confront and transcend schadenfreude.

title: Ping, Latency and Packet Loss Explained: Why Calls and Games Lag
excerpt:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Your video call freezes, your game character t
content:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Your video call freezes, your game character teleports, and someone says "my ping is bad". Here is the simple truth: ping measures how long a tiny message takes to travel to a server and back, latency is that travel time, and packet loss means some messages never arrive at all. A fast download speed cannot fix high latency or packet loss, because they are about the quality of the trip, not the size of the road. This guide explains all three in plain words, shows the numbers that are actually good, and lists the fixes that really work when calls and games lag.

Imagine sending letters. Download speed is how many letters fit in the truck. Latency is how long one letter takes to arrive. Packet loss is letters falling off the truck on the way. A bigger truck does not help if the road is long or the letters keep falling off.

Latency: The Travel Time of Your Data

Latency is the time, in milliseconds (ms), for data to go from your device to a server and back — the round trip. Light itself sets a hard limit: a server on another continent simply cannot answer as fast as one in your own city. Cloudflare's learning centre gives a clear technical walkthrough in its guide on what latency is and what causes it. For everyday use, remember these rough bands: under 30 ms feels instant, 30–60 ms is fine for almost everything, 60–100 ms is noticeable in fast games, and above 150 ms video calls start talking over each other and games feel like they are ignoring you on purpose.

Latency comes from distance, from every router your data hops through, from busy networks queuing your packets like cars at a toll booth, and from Wi-Fi retransmitting data that got garbled in the air. You cannot beat physics, but you can remove the avoidable delays — which is what the fixes below do.

Ping: The Tool That Measures Latency

Ping is both the test and the number it reports. When you run ping google.com in a terminal, your computer sends small ICMP echo requests and times each reply. Games and call apps show "ping" as a live score for the same round-trip idea. One odd high reading means nothing; what matters is the pattern. If your ping sits at 25 ms and suddenly jumps to 400 ms every few seconds, that jumping — called jitter — is often worse than a steady 80 ms, because calls and games can adapt to steady delay but not to surprises. The history and details of the ping utility are on Wikipedia if you enjoy knowing where your tools came from.

Cloudflare's Learning Centre explains latency — the round-trip travel time of your data.

Packet Loss: The Messages That Never Arrive

Data travels in small chunks called packets. Packet loss means some chunks never reach the other side. At 1–2% loss a call sounds robotic and a game stutters; at 5% or more, everything feels broken. The Wikipedia article on packet loss lists the main causes: congested links dropping packets, faulty hardware, weak Wi-Fi signals and overloaded routers. Here is where protocol choice matters: some traffic resends lost packets and some does not. Our comparison of TCP vs UDP explains this in simple words — TCP resends, so a lost packet becomes a delay; live calls and games mostly use UDP-style delivery, so a lost packet becomes a glitch you can hear and see.

That is also why a speed test can look perfect while your call is awful. Speed tests measure big downloads over TCP, which patiently resends everything. They politely hide the packet loss that is ruining your live traffic.

Why Calls and Games Suffer First

Streaming video survives bad networks because it buffers — it downloads the next 30 seconds while you watch the current ones. Calls and games cannot buffer the future. A game must know where you moved now, and a call must play your voice now. So they expose every network flaw instantly: high latency makes actions feel late, jitter makes speech chop in and out, and packet loss erases syllables and teleports players. If Netflix is smooth but your meeting is not, your network is not "fine" — it is fine for buffered things only. The journey your data takes before any of this, by the way, starts the moment you open the app — our guide to what happens when you type a URL covers that first trip in friendly detail.

How to Check Your Own Numbers

Run ping 8.8.8.8 in a terminal for a minute. Read three things: the average time (latency), the spread between lowest and highest (jitter, roughly), and the "packet loss" percentage at the end. Then run the same test plugged into the router with a cable. If the cable numbers are dramatically better, your Wi-Fi is the problem, not your internet plan. Test at different times of day too — a connection that is perfect at 10 am and terrible at 8 pm is suffering from neighbourhood congestion, which no router setting can fully cure.

Fixes That Actually Help

Use a wired connection for calls and games whenever possible — this single change fixes more lag than every other tip combined. If Wi-Fi is unavoidable, move closer to the router, use the 5 GHz band, and keep the router out of cupboards and away from thick walls. Restart the router occasionally. Close heavy background uploads and cloud backups during calls — one phone backing up photos can eat the whole upload side of a home connection. In games, choose the nearest server region, even if your friends picked another one; geography is not negotiable. And if your router offers SQM or QoS settings, enabling them stops one big download from making everyone else's packets queue behind it — the famous "bufferbloat" fix.

Quick Reference: Good and Bad Numbers

Measure Great Okay Trouble
Ping / latency Under 30 ms 30–80 ms Above 150 ms
Jitter Under 5 ms 5–20 ms Above 30 ms
Packet loss 0% Under 1% Above 5%

Keep this little table in mind when you test. One number alone rarely tells the whole story — a 40 ms ping with 8% packet loss feels far worse than a steady 90 ms ping with zero loss. Games and call apps quietly agree: they would rather have your data arrive slightly late than not arrive at all, which is exactly why wired connections, with almost no loss, feel so much better than their speed numbers suggest.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a good ping for gaming?

Under 30 ms is excellent, 30–60 ms is good, and up to 100 ms is playable for most games. Fast competitive shooters feel best below 50 ms. Consistency matters as much as the average.

Why is my ping high but my download speed is fast?

Because speed and latency are different things. Speed is bandwidth — how much data fits per second. Latency is travel time. A wide, long road moves many cars slowly; a narrow, short road moves fewer cars quickly.

How much packet loss is acceptable?

Zero is ideal. Under 1% is usually unnoticeable, 1–2% causes small glitches in calls, and anything above 5% makes calls and games clearly broken.

Does a VPN increase ping?

Almost always, yes. Your data takes a detour through the VPN server, which adds distance and processing. A nearby VPN server adds a little; a far one adds a lot.

Why does my ping spike at night?

Evening congestion. Everyone in your area streams and downloads at once, queues grow at your provider's equipment, and latency plus jitter climb until traffic calms down.

Conclusion

Ping is the measurement, latency is the travel time, and packet loss is data that never arrives. When calls and games lag, do not ask "is my speed fast?" — ask "what are my ping, jitter and loss, on Wi-Fi versus cable?" Test, wire up if you can, pick nearby servers, and tame background uploads. Your future self, mid-meeting and mid-match, will notice the difference immediately.

title: Killing duplicate Telegram posts with idempotent sends and rate limits
excerpt: Our channel bot used to publish the same announcement twice, sometimes three times. Not because the code was clever — because it was naive: a retry after a timeout, a restart halfway through a broa
content:
Our channel bot used to publish the same announcement twice, sometimes three times. Not because the code was clever — because it was naive: a retry after a timeout, a restart halfway through a broadcast, an admin tapping the "publish" button twice. Each of those produced a fresh sendMessage call, and the Bot API happily accepted it.

Here is the setup that fixed it for us. It is roughly 45 minutes of work at an intermediate level, and it is built from three cheap layers: a content fingerprint in SQLite, a per-minute token bucket, and a permalink check after the fact.

The whole flow looks like this:

publisher -> [1] idempotency key -> [2] rate limiter -> [3] sendMessage
                  |                      |                     |
             SQLite outbox          token bucket          message_id
             (UNIQUE key)         (per-minute cap)             |
                  |                                           |
                  +---------- skip on duplicate <--------------+

What you need before you start

Python 3.9+ with requests, a bot token from @botfather, and a private test channel where that bot is an administrator with the "Post messages" permission. Note both the numeric channel id (-100...) and the public username, since both end up in the code. Keep the Bot API docs open in a tab — the limits below are what we worked with, but Telegram adjusts them, so verify the current numbers before you hardcode production values.

mkdir -p ~/tg-dedup && cd ~/tg-dedup
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests

export TG_BOT_TOKEN="<token-from-BotFather>"
export TG_CHANNEL="-1001234567890"
export TG_CHANNEL_USER="my_test_channel"

The token lives in an environment variable and never in the repository. Quick sanity check: echo "${TG_BOT_TOKEN:0:10}" should print the first ten characters.

Layer 1: fingerprint the content, not the click

An idempotency key is a fingerprint of an operation. Run the same operation twice, get the same fingerprint, and the second run is thrown away instead of executed. For us the fingerprint is a SHA-256 hash of the channel id plus the normalized message text, truncated to 32 hex characters.

Normalization matters more than the hash. Collapsing whitespace and lowercasing means "Hello World" and "hello world" produce one key — which is exactly the duplicate we kept getting from a re-rendered template.

# dedup.py
import hashlib
import sqlite3

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS outbox (
    idem_key   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    channel_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    text       TEXT NOT NULL,
    status     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',   -- pending | sent | failed
    message_id INTEGER,
    attempts   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
    sent_at    TEXT
);
"""


def idempotency_key(channel_id: str, text: str) -> str:
    normalized = " ".join(text.split()).strip().lower()
    raw = f"{channel_id}:{normalized}".encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()[:32]


def init_db(path: str = "outbox.db") -> None:
    con = sqlite3.connect(path)
    con.executescript(SCHEMA)
    con.commit()
    con.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    init_db()

Check that normalization actually works before moving on:

python3 dedup.py
python3 -c "
from dedup import idempotency_key
print(idempotency_key('-1001234567890', 'Hello  World'))
print(idempotency_key('-1001234567890', 'hello world'))
"

Both lines must be identical 32-character hex strings. If they differ, your normalization is broken and every downstream layer is decoration.

Layer 2: let SQLite decide who wins

Because idem_key is the TEXT PRIMARY KEY, the database itself becomes the arbiter. The second insert of the same key conflicts, and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING turns that conflict into a silent no-op. Two processes cannot both walk away thinking they own the message.

def claim(key: str, text: str) -> bool:
    """Insert first; False means someone already owns this key."""
    con = sqlite3.connect(DB)
    cur = con.execute(
        "INSERT INTO outbox (idem_key, channel_id, text) VALUES (?, ?, ?) "
        "ON CONFLICT(idem_key) DO NOTHING",
        (key, CHANNEL, text),
    )
    con.commit()
    claimed = cur.rowcount == 1
    con.close()
    return claimed

The ordering is the point: the row is written before the network call, not after. If the process dies between the insert and the send, you are left with an explicit pending row you can inspect and decide about — instead of an invisible duplicate you find out about from a subscriber.

Layer 3: a token bucket plus retry_after

One thing worth internalizing: sendMessage has no idempotency parameter. Deduplication is entirely your job (confirm the current parameter list in the docs). The second part of the job is not getting throttled during a broadcast loop.

The limiter below is a token bucket — it keeps timestamps of recent sends and sleeps when the per-minute cap is reached. We sized it at 20 per minute for a single channel, based on the documented figure of roughly 20 messages per minute per group or channel and a global cap near 30 messages per second.

# publisher.py
import os
import sqlite3
import sys
import time

import requests

from dedup import idempotency_key, init_db

BOT_TOKEN = os.environ["TG_BOT_TOKEN"]
CHANNEL = os.environ["TG_CHANNEL"]
USERNAME = os.environ["TG_CHANNEL_USER"]
API = f"https://api.telegram.org/bot{BOT_TOKEN}"
DB = "outbox.db"


class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, per_minute: int = 20):
        self.per_minute = per_minute
        self.stamps = []

    def wait(self) -> None:
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.stamps = [t for t in self.stamps if now - t < 60]
        if len(self.stamps) >= self.per_minute:
            time.sleep(60 - (now - self.stamps[0]) + 0.5)
        self.stamps.append(time.monotonic())


def publish(text: str, limiter: RateLimiter) -> None:
    key = idempotency_key(CHANNEL, text)
    if not claim(key, text):
        print(f"skip: duplicate idem_key={key}")
        return

    r = None
    for _ in range(3):
        limiter.wait()
        r = requests.post(
            f"{API}/sendMessage",
            json={"chat_id": CHANNEL, "text": text, "disable_web_page_preview": True},
            timeout=15,
        )
        if r.status_code != 429:
            break
        retry_after = r.json().get("parameters", {}).get("retry_after", 30)
        print(f"429: sleeping {retry_after}s")
        time.sleep(retry_after)

    body = r.json()
    if not body.get("ok"):
        print(f"failed: {body.get('description')}")
        return

    message_id = body["result"]["message_id"]
    con = sqlite3.connect(DB)
    con.execute(
        "UPDATE outbox SET status='sent', message_id=?, sent_at=datetime('now') "
        "WHERE idem_key=?",
        (message_id, key),
    )
    con.commit()
    con.close()
    print(f"sent: message_id={message_id} https://t.me/{USERNAME}/{message_id}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    init_db()
    publish(" ".join(sys.argv[1:]), RateLimiter(per_minute=20))

The retry loop gives up after three attempts, and it reads retry_after from the response instead of using a fixed sleep. That detail is what stops a second 429 from landing one second after the first.

Step 4: confirm the post is really there

Run it once:

python3 publisher.py "Hello from the outbox"

Expected output:

sent: message_id=42 https://t.me/my_test_channel/42

Then open the permalink. This third layer is the one people skip: an HTTP 200 only proves Telegram accepted something. A permalink check is what catches a wrong channel id, a wrong username, or a post that was deleted right after publishing.

sqlite3 outbox.db "SELECT status, message_id FROM outbox;"

Run the script again with the same text and you should see skip: duplicate idem_key=... and no new row.

Things I keep an eye on

  • Limits drift. The 30/sec global and ~20/min per-channel figures were accurate when I built this; re-read the docs before setting production values.
  • One worker only. The token bucket lives in process memory, so it does nothing for you across multiple workers. Run a single publisher and queue the work.
  • Failed sends stay visible. A pending row after a crash is a feature, not a bug — but somebody has to look at it and decide whether to retry.
  • Environment variables, always. The token in a shell export is boring and that is precisely why it works.

What I took away

Duplicate posts are rarely a Telegram problem. They are an ordering problem: we called the network before we recorded the intent, so the system had no memory of what it had already done. Writing the intent first, letting a unique key arbitrate, throttling to a documented rate, and verifying with a permalink cost us a table and about 90 lines of Python — and the duplicates stopped.

If you want more write-ups like this one, this article was originally published on AI Release — https://ai-release.org. There is also a channel with new guides at https://t.me/ai_release1.

title: The Ghost in the Machine: A Haunted AI Shell Wrapper for Developers
excerpt:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Wh
content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every developer knows the sudden, cold dread of running a broken command right before a deadline: an untracked branch, a mangled flag, or a syntax error spit back by an uncaring compiler.

To celebrate Halloween and Día de los Muertos, I brought that unseen presence to life by building Ghost in the Machine (Ghost-Shell)—a possessed terminal wrapper infused with open-source AI.

Instead of plain, dry stack traces, an ancient spirit haunts your keystrokes from deep within your motherboard:

  • Spectral Error Divination: When any shell command fails (returncode != 0), the ghost intercepts stderr, analyses the failure through open-weight models, and whispers a spooky diagnosis alongside a concrete fixing Ritual (the exact command needed to solve it).
  • The Día de los Muertos seance: Type seance, and the wrapper lights digital marigolds. It reads your project's recent git commit history or oldest abandoned files, composing a poetic digital ofrenda to honor the code and experiments that came before.
  • Possessed Shell Behavior: Features retro ASCII ghost art, typewriter-speed ghostly whispers in glowing terminal colors, ambient eerie commentary on successful tasks, and custom traps (you can't just Ctrl+C a spirit—you have to type exorcise to banish it).

Demo

Here is the spirit intervening after a typo, guiding the fix, and communing with the repository's ancestors via seance:

Code

Shadow16Ua / Ghost-Shell

How I Built It

Ghost-Shell is built in lightweight, dependency-minimal Python utilizing high-throughput open-weight models (openai/gpt-oss-20b and qwen/qwen3.8-27b) served via Groq:

  1. Subprocess Execution & Interception: The interactive loop executes native system binaries while capturing standard streams (stdout and stderr).
  2. Contextual Spirit Analysis: When execution fails, the script packages the working directory context, the invoked command, and the error log into a structured prompt with response_format={"type": "json_object"}. The open-weight model acts as a two-part entity: generating a thematic narrative (whisper) while calculating deterministic repair instructions (ritual).
  3. Ancestral Archaeology (seance): The tool extracts the repository's past through git log -n 5 --oneline (or file modification timestamps) and prompts the model to generate a reflective, respectful remembrance honoring legacy development.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Building an ambient assistant that monitors shell commands makes open innovation and open weights essential:

  • Command Privacy & Shell Security: Shell commands frequently contain local file paths, environment variable references, internal IPs, and sensitive developer workflows. Routing those through open-weight inference guarantees that private development environments aren't stored or used to train proprietary third-party systems.
  • Instant Ambient Latency: Having an eerie AI voice feel responsive in a terminal requires sub-second generation. Fast, open models like gpt-oss-20b running on optimized inference engines produce instant responses, making the ghost feel genuinely alive rather than like an API waiting room.
  • Model Independence: Because the tool targets standard open-weight architectures, developers are free to swap from cloud inference to local, completely offline inference (via Ollama or vLLM) so the spirit still speaks even when the power and internet are completely severed.

My Agent Session

The Spirit of It

The moment this project truly came alive wasn’t just watching the terminal catch typos with eerie metaphors—it was testing the seance command on an abandoned folder of old scripts from my early coding days.

Seeing the open-weight model parse messy, forgotten commit messages and weave them into a respectful, poetic tribute felt surprisingly grounded. In tech, we are conditioned to constantly delete, deprecate, and refactor the past away. Lighting a digital candle on an altar of legacy code turned debugging from a source of frustration into a celebratory reflection on how far we've come as developers.

And, of course, hitting Ctrl+C in panic only to be told "You cannot Ctrl+C a ghost... Type 'exorcise' to leave" delivered exactly the subtle chill every developer terminal needs in late October.

Prize Categories

  • Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4 (Ghost in the Machine)

title: AI agent payments usually get the flow right and the trust wrong
excerpt: Over the last two weeks I kept running into AI agent payment projects: a pay-per-call facilitator, a swap API built for agents, a test suite for x402 payments, a guard that sits between an agent an
content:
Over the last two weeks I kept running into AI agent payment projects: a pay-per-call facilitator, a swap API built for agents, a test suite for x402 payments, a guard that sits between an agent and its wallet, and a banking agent.

The payments worked in all five. The gap was somewhere else, in something the payment path trusted without checking, and it was never the model.

Every team took the feedback well and most shipped a fix within days, so this isn't about anyone being careless. It's a blind spot that's easy to have when the model gets all the attention.

Who decides where the money goes

An x402 facilitator live on mainnet gives each merchant their own vault contract, which pulls the payment and splits it in one transaction, the net to the merchant and the fee to the protocol.

To change where a vault pays, the merchant has to sign. That's the strong control. But the operator deploys the vault, and the first payout address comes from what was saved in the dashboard. The docs call that setting a preference, not an authority. You only see that it decides the first payments in the vault code, not in the docs.

So the weaker path picks where the money goes, and the merchant's signature only matters after that. If the operator key leaks, every merchant who hasn't been paid yet can get a vault that pays someone else.

The dev agreed and is fixing it so operator-created vaults always pay the merchant. If you ever fix something like this, remember the payout is written once, when the vault is created. A fix in the factory only covers new vaults. The existing ones keep whatever they were given, so you go through the creation events and ask those merchants to confirm.

If the address comes from the API, it's not a check

Then there was a free swap API and MCP server for agents. It asks several aggregators and bridges for quotes, ranks the routes and returns calldata, and the agent signs whatever comes back.

That makes the upstream APIs part of the agent's wallet. If one of them is compromised, it can hand back calldata that sends the swap to someone else, and every agent using the API signs it.

I suggested decoding the calldata on the server first: the router is on an allowlist, the recipient is the user, and the minimum output matches the quote. They shipped it within a day.

Then they hit the harder case, a bridge where the recipient is bound off chain. Their fix was good: fetch the order, recompute its id, check the recipient and the minimum amount, and require the deposit to go to the bridge's deposit contract. But the deposit contract address came from the same bridge API at runtime. A compromised API could list its own contract, and every order check would still pass, because the funds never reach the real one.

Pin addresses like that per chain in your config, and alert when the API disagrees.

"A payment exists" is not "this payment paid for this"

This one is an open-source CI suite that injects faults into x402 settlement on Solana, so a server can test how it handles bad payments. The author asked which checks were missing.

I'd start with a valid payment made for a cheaper route, or to a different recipient, replayed against a pricier route. A server that only checks that a settled payment exists will serve it.

They took it as tests for amount, recipient and resource substitution. Then I asked about the same amount paid in a different token, or on devnet, replayed against a mainnet route. Checks that only compare amount and recipient let that through. They shipped both as new checks in their next release.

The same thing comes up on the client side. In x402 the 402 response tells the agent which token contract and which network to pay on. So a spend limit that pins the recipient but not the asset and the network can be walked around by an endpoint that keeps the number the same and changes the token. And when a human approves a payment, they should see the exact requirements that get signed, not the agent's summary of them.

The signature your guard doesn't know about

An open-source guard for agent wallets holds unlimited approvals, Permit signatures and long expiries by default, which are the ones that usually bite.

The one missing was EIP-7702. An authorization is a signature over a chain id, an address and a nonce. It isn't typed data and it isn't a normal transaction, but it delegates the whole account to a contract, which is worse than any unlimited approval. And a chain id of 0 makes it valid on every chain.

The guard approved a type 4 transaction even when its authorization list delegated the account, and the framework plugin didn't look at the authorization list at all. The author fixed both and published within three hours.

He was also honest about the limit: the guard only sees what goes through the wrapped client. If the agent can reach the raw key, nothing on the client side sees the authorization. One thing a guard can still do on its own is read its account's code before each send. A delegated account returns 0xef0100 followed by the delegate's address. If that points somewhere you don't expect, stop signing.

The text the model still writes

The banking agent was already well built. The customer types the payee and the amount, and the confirm screen sits outside the chat, so the model can't misdescribe the transfer.

But the transfer note is still written by the model, and it leaves the bank and lands with someone outside. A model that read a malicious message can put the customer's balance or another account number in the note of a small transfer. It's the same problem as email tools where the recipient is pinned but the model writes the body.

The simplest fix I can think of is a note field on the confirm screen that the customer fills in. Then the model never writes it.

What I check now

These are the questions I ask about an agent payment design now:

  1. Who can set where the money goes, and in what order? If a weaker control decides first and the strong one only applies later, the weak one is the real control.
  2. Where does every address come from? If it comes from the same API you're checking, it's not a check. Pin it.
  3. What is the payment bound to? Amount, recipient, resource, token and network. Not just "a settled payment exists".
  4. Which signatures can the agent's key produce? Transactions, typed data, permits and EIP-7702 authorizations. A guard that only knows some of them isn't a guard for the others.
  5. What free text does the model still write that reaches someone outside? Notes, memos, email bodies, metadata. That's a way to send data out.

None of the fixes needed a smarter model.

If you're building agent payments, I'm curious which address in your flow still comes from an API you don't control.

I first wrote a short version of this on X.

I wrote this with help from AI for drafting and editing. The opinions and the review experience are mine.

title: New Models Move Fast. Your API Integration Should Not Need to Start Over
content:
Model news moved again this week. OpenAI published an updated Model Spec on October 29, while Mistral announced that Mistral Large 4 is now open weight. Add the recent Carbon and Genie announcements, and one engineering lesson becomes clear: model capabilities move faster than most application code should. OpenAI update · Mistral announcement.\n\nRelayRouter is useful here because the application can begin from one documented gateway, one server-side credential pattern, and one request contract for supported routes. The model identifier still changes, and every route must be checked in the current console, but the surrounding integration does not need to be rebuilt for every headline.\n\nThe practical goal is not to call every new model on day one. It is to make model selection, fallback, validation, and review explicit enough that a team can change routes without losing control of the workflow.

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, emphasizing long tasks and cyberdefense, with a staged initial rollout. That makes this a good moment to revisit the application design around extended AI work. Official announcement.

This tutorial is a design you can start building with a text route available to your RelayRouter account. It is not a Carbon access guide or a claim that Carbon is available through the gateway.

1. Turn a broad request into a reviewable unit

“Prepare the product launch” mixes research, writing, asset production, and publication. If an agent stops halfway through, the application cannot infer which pieces are complete from a confident final sentence.

Narrow the first task to a product-page draft from approved facts. For a synthetic ceramic cup, those facts might be 300 mL, ivory, and hand-wash only. The useful output is a proposed draft and a checklist that another person can inspect. No one needs to publish anything during this first experiment.

Give the task a durable identifier. Keep the original brief, an input revision, and the latest approved artifact together. A model's conversational memory should not be the only place where your workflow state exists.

2. Separate a proposal from completed work

Use distinct states such as requested, draft_ready, review_needed, and approved. Decide which events are allowed to change them. A model can propose that a draft is ready; an application check or reviewer should establish whether the transition is valid.

For example, a checklist might ask whether the capacity is preserved, whether care instructions are accurate, and whether unsupported claims were introduced. A generated checklist is still a proposal. It is not evidence that those checks ran.

The downloadable Python example deliberately produces only that proposal. Its response contract has two fields:

{
  "task": "Review the ceramic cup draft",
  "checks": [
    "Confirm the stated capacity is 300 mL.",
    "Keep the hand-wash-only instruction.",
    "Remove claims not supported by the approved brief."
  ]
}

This is an illustrative expected shape, not a recorded model response. The local validator checks the exact field names, text types, three-item list, and field lengths. A human still needs to judge whether the proposed checks are useful.

3. Make the first API connection

Create an API key and select a documented text route in the current RelayRouter console. Copy its Base URL and model identifier rather than guessing an ID from a headline. Keep the key on the server.

Set these variables locally, then run the included request_checklist.py:

export RELAYROUTER_BASE_URL='COPY_HTTPS_BASE_URL_FROM_CONSOLE'
export RELAYROUTER_API_KEY='YOUR_SERVER_SIDE_KEY'
export RELAYROUTER_MODEL='AVAILABLE_TEXT_MODEL_ID'
python request_checklist.py

The script uses Python's standard library. It appends /chat/completions to the Base URL, sends one non-streaming text request, checks normal completion, and parses the result. Use a route that documents support for that request shape. A world simulation or a provider-hosted agent is a different product surface.

The key request instructions are intentionally modest:

payload = {
    "model": model,
    "stream": False,
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "Propose a review checklist. Return only JSON with exactly task (a short string) and checks (exactly three short strings). These are proposed checks, not completed work. Do not claim to have executed tests or changed files."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Synthetic brief: draft a product page for an unbranded ceramic cup. Approved facts: 300 mL, ivory, hand-wash only. Suggest checks for factual fidelity, instructions, and review readiness."
        }
    ]
}

The complete example has response validation and error handling. This excerpt only shows the payload. Neither version executes tools, edits a repository, or publishes a page.

4. Save evidence at the boundary

After a successful response, record the task identifier, input revision, requested model, available response metadata, and the artifact awaiting review. Keep status separate from prose. If a reviewer rejects the draft, preserve the reason and the version they reviewed.

For a coding task, evidence might include a patch, the exact tests actually run, and their results. For a content task, it might include approved source facts and corrections. Do not let a model-written claim that tests passed replace actual test output.

Use the smallest record that makes a failure understandable. Avoid storing credentials or unrestricted customer text in general logs. Decide the appropriate retention policy for the actual application data.

5. Design resumption before adding more steps

Suppose the request times out. The client knows it stopped waiting; it does not necessarily know whether upstream computation ended. Avoid silently starting the entire workflow again, especially after side effects.

The application should inspect its last confirmed checkpoint and decide whether it can safely retry a pure generation step. Actions such as sending a message or updating an invoice need stronger reconciliation and duplicate-prevention rules. Those are application responsibilities, not consequences of choosing a larger model.

The practical value of RelayRouter is the API connection for supported routes while your own workflow defines completion. Start with one available route, one proposed artifact, and one reviewer. Build a record of progress that will still make sense after the conversation ends.

title: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech
content:
What do drones, routers, and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones from entering the country. They’re the first consumer gadgets that are facing de facto import bans because of the US government’s xenophobic stance — and they might not be the last.

Originally, the US government was just worried about US networks. It’s been distrustful of Chinese telecom equipment providers Huawei and ZTE for well over a decade, eventually requiring telecom providers to “rip and replace” their gear. (Many telecoms have still failed to do so.) It established an “Entity List” for companies whose gear should be banned from import, marketing, and sale.

But under the second Trump administration, that list has been weaponized against entire home consumer gadget categories too — starting in December 2025 when Trump and Brendan Carr’s FCC banned all future foreign drones unless their companies obtained a waiver.

Next was a ban on all future foreign routers, all future foreign robots and power inverters, and within the robot ban, all future foreign robovacs. In each case, the government claims it’s because those gadgets fundamentally pose an unacceptable threat to US national security. But in each case, the US has provided zero public evidence of a threat, has done nothing about existing drones and routers and robots that might pose such a threat, and hasn’t given us any reason to trust that its waivers have anything to do with security.

Besides, there are rarely any US companies to fill the gaps left by foreign ones. Consumer gadgets are largely made overseas, including practically all routers and practically all drones — just like how your Apple, Dell, and HP laptops are not made in the US.

In this StoryStream, we’re following the latest on the foreign gadget bans.

content:
Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Submission 🕯️

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Séance — an offline séance chatbot that channels the spirits of dead programming languages (COBOL, FORTRAN, ALGOL, LISP, Smalltalk, Ada, Prolog) through Gemma, a local open-weight model. It works with the lights and the internet off, and every séance stays on your machine — nothing is uploaded to a server you don't control.

Repo: mahilsaily306-max/seance

Demo

Deployed frontend: (link goes here — render / digitalocean / .tech domain)

Demo video: (link goes here)

Core flows, one click each:

Conjure a spirit → pick COBOL, FORTRAN, LISP, or any of the seven dead languages and ask it questions
One-shot conjure → node src/seance.js --spirit COBOL --ask "What is a paragraph?"
Interactive séance → chat mode with past-séance history replay
History → replay previous turns for a summoned spirit
Voice → ElevenLabs TTS reads the spirit's whisper aloud (optional)

Code

mahilsaily306-max/seance

Key files:

src/seance.js — CLI séance: conjure spirits, chat, log turns, replay history
src/spirits.js — the seven dead-language spirits, each with era, epitaph, style, last words
src/model.js — Gemma local client (Ollama / Hugging Face / offline echo fallback)
src/memory.js — MongoDB Atlas vector memory with Tiger Data / pgvector fallback
src/tracing.js — Sentry agent tracing (latency, source, errors)
src/search.js — SerpApi live web search for historical language facts (optional)
src/voice.js — ElevenLabs TTS for spirit whispers (optional)
src/session.js — Durable Temporal-style sessions logged to JSONL
scripts/setup.js — one-time dependency setup
docker-compose.yml — local MongoDB stack for offline memory

How I Built It

Open-source AI at every layer:

Runtime: Gemma (open-weight) via Ollama; falls back to a deterministic offline echo so the séance runs with zero ML installs and zero internet.
Memory: JSONL local log (Temporal-style durability) so séances survive restarts; optionally MongoDB Atlas vector memory or Tiger Data/pgvector hybrid search over past turns.
Tracing: Sentry captures agent setup, latency, tokens, cost, and errors — set SENTRY_DSN and every turn is traced.
Search: SerpApi grounds answers in fresh web results when you want historical language context.
Voice: ElevenLabs TTS gives the spirits a voice; the séance works silently without it.
CI: npm test exercises every module; works with no dependencies installed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Running open-weight models locally means:

No internet needed. Gemma runs on a laptop offline after download. A closed API agent would stop working without connectivity.
Data stays on your machine. Your séance logs, questions, and answers are never uploaded to a server you don't control.
Set up once, never pay again. Open-weight models cost $0 to run locally — no per-token charges, no subscriptions.
Swap models freely. Swap Gemma for Mistral, Llama, or any open weight. Closed APIs lock you into one vendor.
The open-based approach worked better here because this is a personal, offline-first tool — privacy, offline use, and zero recurring cost matter more than a hosted SaaS.

My Agent Session

Saved with DevRelay and embedded below (Entire prize category: share the agent sessions behind your project).

(agent_session embed link goes here)

The Spooky Payoff

Before Séance, dead programming languages were just forgotten syntax in dusty manuals — COBOL, FORTRAN, LISP, Smalltalk, Ada, Prolog, buried by the industry.

title: I built a free, privacy-first 8th Pay Commission pension calculator as a static site
excerpt: India's 8th Central Pay Commission will revise pensions for roughly 69 lakh central government pensioners. Most "calculators" online are ad-heavy, English-only, or don't show their formulas. So I b
content:
India's 8th Central Pay Commission will revise pensions for roughly 69 lakh central government pensioners. Most "calculators" online are ad-heavy, English-only, or don't show their formulas. So I built one that runs entirely in the browser.

Live: https://8cpc-pension-calculator.vercel.app/ (Hindi: https://8cpc-pension-calculator.vercel.app/hi/)

What it does

  • New basic pension at every projected fitment factor (1.92 to 3.833)
  • DA/DR with arrears, family pension, commutation and 15-year restoration
  • A page for each pension amount, e.g. ₹25,000 pension in 8th Pay Commission
  • Every figure linked to official orders (PIB, DoPPW, Pensioners' Portal)

How it's built

  • Plain HTML generated by a small Python build script: no framework, no runtime server
  • Vanilla JS for the calculations, so nothing leaves the user's device
  • A full server-rendered Hindi counterpart for every page, with reciprocal hreflang
  • Strict CSP, JSON-LD (FAQPage, WebApplication), a sitemap, IndexNow pings, and llms.txt for AI crawlers
  • Deployed on Vercel from GitHub, with tests run before each push

Lessons

  1. Server-rendered language versions beat JS toggles for SEO.
  2. Showing the formula and its source builds more trust than a fancy UI.
  3. Keep titles under 70 characters and descriptions under 160. Bing flags both.

I also built YT Policy Shield, a free YouTube monetization-policy and AI-voice risk checker, with the same static approach.

Feedback welcome!
